params.question: A patient's wound has entered the proliferative phase. Which of the following processes would you expect to observe in the wound at this stage?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Platelet aggregation and fibrin clot formation describe haemostasis, the first phase, occurring within seconds of injury — not the proliferative phase.
Neutrophil infiltration is characteristic of the early inflammatory phase (days 1–5). By the proliferative phase, macrophages have taken over as the dominant cell.

answers.text: Angiogenesis, collagen deposition by fibroblasts, and epithelialisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The proliferative phase (day 3 to approximately 3 weeks) is characterised by new capillary growth (angiogenesis), type III collagen laid down by fibroblasts, and epithelial cells migrating across the wound surface.

answers.text: Replacement of type III collagen by organised type I collagen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Collagen remodelling — replacing weaker type III with stronger type I — occurs during the remodelling (maturation) phase, which spans months to about two years after injury.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the four phases. The proliferative phase (day 3–3 weeks) is characterised by fibroblast collagen deposition, angiogenesis, and epithelialisation — building the new tissue that fills the wound.
Well done. Recognising what each phase contributes is the foundation for understanding wound healing complications.

interactions.label: A 62-year-old with poorly controlled diabetes, malnutrition, and a heavy smoking

params.question: A 62-year-old with poorly controlled diabetes, malnutrition, and a heavy smoking habit has a wound showing deficient collagen deposition after two weeks. Which combination of factors most directly explains this finding?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both impair healing, but leucocyte dysfunction primarily blunts the inflammatory phase. Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow but does not directly remove the substrates that collagen synthesis requires.

answers.text: Malnutrition (protein and vitamin C deficiency) and smoking (tissue hypoxia)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Collagen synthesis requires protein for structure, vitamin C as the cofactor for cross-linking, and adequate oxygen. Malnutrition removes the substrates; smoking imposes tissue hypoxia. Together, they most directly explain deficient collagen deposition.

Malnutrition does contribute, but the key substrates collagen depends on are protein and vitamin C — not zinc alone. Diabetic microvascular disease affects perfusion, not collagen substrate availability directly.

Age and diabetes both slow healing through reduced cellular activity and poor perfusion, but they do not directly explain the lack of collagen substrates. The nutritional deficit is the more direct cause of poor collagen deposition.

overallFeedback.feedback: When analysing poor collagen deposition, identify what collagen synthesis needs: protein (substrate), vitamin C (cofactor for cross-linking), and oxygen. Then find which patient factors deprive the wound of these.
Excellent analysis. Tracing a clinical finding to its most direct cause — here, substrate and oxygen deprivation for collagen synthesis — is a key clinical reasoning skill.

interactions.label: An elective cholecystectomy is performed. The biliary tract is opened under cont

params.question: An elective cholecystectomy is performed. The biliary tract is opened under controlled conditions and closed without spillage. Under the CDC wound classification, this wound falls into which class?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A Class I (clean) wound has no hollow viscus entered. Since the biliary tract was opened during this procedure, the wound cannot be classified as clean.

Correct. Class II (clean-contaminated) applies when a hollow viscus is entered under controlled conditions without unusual contamination. The biliary tract was opened and closed without spillage, placing this in Class II with an infection risk of approximately 3–5%.
Class III (contaminated) involves a major break in sterile technique, gross spillage from a hollow viscus, or fresh traumatic wounds. A controlled entry without spillage does not meet these criteria.
Class IV (dirty/infected) requires established infection, devitalised tissue, or old traumatic wounds with retained dead tissue. An elective procedure without spillage is far below this threshold.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the four CDC classes: Clean (no viscus entered), Clean-contaminated (controlled viscus entry), Contaminated (traumatic or major spillage), Dirty (established infection). A controlled biliary tract entry without spillage is Class II.
Correct. The CDC classification guides both closure decisions and antibiotic strategy — higher class means higher infection risk and a stronger argument against primary closure.

params.question: A patient presents to the emergency department with a wound to the abdomen. Which of the following descriptions is most appropriate for medicolegal documentation?

answers.text: "Stab wound, 3 cm, in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen"

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Calling it a 'stab wound' is an interpretation of causation, not an observation. Courts require objective description of what you see, without assuming the mechanism of injury.

answers.text: "Penetrating wound, 3 cm long with clean margins, located 5 cm left of the umbilicus"

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This describes wound type (penetrating), dimensions (3 cm), edge character (clean margins), and site using a fixed anatomical landmark (umbilicus) — all objective observations, with no interpretation of causation.

answers.text: "Deep wound caused by a sharp weapon, left side of abdomen"

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: "Caused by a sharp weapon" is interpretation, not observation. "Left side of abdomen" lacks a precise anatomical landmark. Medicolegal records must describe objectively using fixed reference points.

answers.text: "Small wound, left abdomen, consistent with knife injury"

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: "Small" is subjective — record dimensions instead. "Consistent with knife injury" interprets causation. Medicolegal documentation must use measurable, objective terms and fixed anatomical landmarks.

overallFeedback.feedback: In medicolegal documentation, describe what you observe: exact site using fixed anatomical landmarks, dimensions in centimetres, and wound characteristics. Never interpret the mechanism or cause of injury.
Exactly right. Objective, landmark-based wound description — site, dimensions, edge character — is fundamental to medicolegal documentation.
